Stage 3 · Grammar

Asking the right question

The word order that works in every tense.

Read these four questions.
  • Where do you live?
  • What are you doing this weekend?
  • What did you do at the weekend?
  • How long have you known each other?
In all four questions, what comes straight after the question word?
The order
TenseQuestion wordHelping verbPersonMain verb + rest
Present SimpleWheredoyoulive?
Present Simple (he/she)Whatdoesyour sisterdo?
Present ContinuousWhatareyoudoing this weekend?
Past SimpleWhatdidyoudo at the weekend?
Present PerfectHow longhaveyouknown each other?
Yes / No question—Doyouenjoy museums?
Negative questionWhydon’tyouask her?
Asking about the personWho lives with you?  —  here who is the person, so there is no helping verb.
Short answersDo you? → Yes, I do. / No, I don’t. · Did she? → Yes, she did. · Have you? → Yes, I have.
Repeat the helping verb — never the main verb. Not Yes, I live.
helping verb person

FORM. (question word) + helping verb + person + main verb — the order never changes. The helping verb carries the tense, so the main verb stays in its simple form: did you go, not did you went.

USE. do / does = routines and facts · am / is / are = happening now or arranged · did = finished time · have / has = a period still open.

SHORT ANSWERS. Repeat the helping verb, not the main verb: Do you live here? → Yes, I do. Not Yes, I live.

Not “Where you live?”, not “What did you went?”, not “How long you know her?”

Question forms come back with the past continuous in Lesson 8.

FORM. Question word first, then the helping verb, then the person, then the main verb: How long · have · you · lived here? English keeps this order in every tense. The helping verb carries the tense and the main verb does not — that is why we say did you go and not did you went, and does she work and not does she works.

Choose the helping verb from the tense you need: do / does for the present simple (routines and facts), am / is / are for the present continuous (right now, or arranged), did for the past simple (finished time), have / has for the present perfect (a period that is still open, often with how long).

The three mistakes to watch: “Where you live?” (no helping verb) · “What did you went?” (tense twice) · “How long you know her?” (missing have).

Short answers repeat the helping verb, never the main verb. Do you live here? → Yes, I do. / No, I don’t.   Did she call? → Yes, she did.   Have you finished? → Yes, I have. Saying Yes, I live sounds wrong to a native speaker, even though the meaning is clear.

Two things to file away. When the question word is the person — Who lives with you?, What happened? — you do not add a helping verb. And a negative question softens a suggestion: Why don’t you ask her? means I think you should. Question forms come back with the past continuous in Lesson 8.

Real questions from the coursebook recording.

Full grammar reference — Question forms

Form

Yes/No, presentDo you live here? · Does she work? · Are you busy?
Yes/No, pastDid you go out? · Were you late?
Wh- questionWhere do you live? · What did she say?
Subject questionWho lives here? · What happened? (no auxiliary)
Short answersYes, I do. / No, she doesn’t. · Yes, I did. / No, we weren’t.

When and why we use it

  • The normal order is (question word) + auxiliary + subject + main verb: Where do you go at the weekend?
  • With be there is no do. The verb itself moves in front of the subject: Are you ready?
  • When the question word is the subject, keep normal word order and use no auxiliary: Who called you?, not Who did call you?
  • How combines with other words: How long, How often, How much, How many, How old.

Signal words

what · where · when · who · why · which · whose · how (long / often / much / many / old)

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • Where you live? → Where do you live?A question needs an auxiliary before the subject.
  • Did you went out? → Did you go out?After did the main verb is always plain.
  • What she does? → What does she do?Auxiliary first, then the subject.
  • Who did call you? → Who called you?Who is the subject here, so no did.

Don’t confuse it with

Do or are? Use do/does with ordinary verbs (Do you study here?) and am/is/are with be (Are you a student?).

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

The main text of the lesson.

Before you read: two strangers sit in a room and ask each other 36 personal questions for 45 minutes.

Do you think they feel closer afterwards? Decide first, then read and find out if you were right.

There is no right answer here. This is your prediction.

Three sets of questions

In 1997 an American psychologist called Arthur Aron tried an experiment. He put two strangers in a room and gave them a list of thirty-six questions. They had forty-five minutes. The questions came in three sets, and each set was more personal than the last. The first set was easy: Who is your dream dinner guest? The last set was not: When did you last cry in front of another person?

Another group of strangers got small talk instead — the weather, work, family, favourite food. What did you do at the weekend? Do you like this weather?

Aron’s team then recorded how close each pair felt. The result surprised everyone. The pairs who asked the thirty-six questions felt much closer than the small-talk pairs, and many of them said they felt as close to this stranger as they did in their closest relationships. One pair from that first experiment later got married.

Twenty-five years later, other researchers asked more than 1,800 people to have one shallow conversation and one deep one. Before they started, most people expected to prefer the small talk. Afterwards, most people preferred the deep conversation.

So why do we still chat about the weather? Partly because we are busy. But mostly because we are wrong: we think other people are not interested in our real answers.

You can still find the thirty-six questions online, and people share them in posts and send them to friends by text every year. The researchers were careful, though. Nobody made a promise that strangers would become friends. The questions worked in a laboratory, with two people who had agreed to take part and who both knew the rules.

Sources. Aron, Melinat, Aron, Vallone & Bator (1997), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 23(4) · Kardas, Kumar & Epley (2022), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Text written for this course.
